title: To share or not to share - The underlying motives of sharing fake news amidst the COVID-19 pandemic in Malaysia
screen_reason: Survey of 869 Malaysians on the motives for sharing fake news. The aim is motives (SEM), which by itself would not qualify, but the sample-description table (Table 4) reports one descriptive share tied to the misinformation construct: 19/869 (2.2%) say the action they take on suspicious news is to share/forward it immediately - a self-reported sharing share with a denominator (RECALL, recall_subtype sharing). The paper's fake-news-sharing scale items ('I have shared/spread fake news before knowingly / unknowingly') are reported only as factor loadings and path coefficients, never as a share of respondents, so they yield no row. INCLUDE is borderline and rests entirely on that one table cell; an adjudicator who judges 'suspicious news' too far from 'misinformation' should EXCLUDE the paper as motives/SEM-only.

estimates.platform: Online self-administered questionnaire (Google Form distributed via Facebook and WhatsApp)
estimates.date: Not stated; respondents were asked about their personal experiences since January 2020; manuscript received 28 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents whose reported action on suspicious news is to share/forward it immediately
estimates.denominator: 869 Malaysian online survey respondents aged 18-59 (mean age 22.7; 80.6% tertiary students; 59.7% female)
estimates.definition: Respondent chose 'Share/Forward immediately' from the single-choice list of actions taken on suspicious news (the alternatives were Ignore, Fact-checking website, Google verification, Family/friends verification)
estimates.misinfo_def: "The present study redefines fake news as 'misleading or incorrect information in any forms, disseminated intentionally or unintentionally'. In other words, fake news is deemed to encompass misinformation, disinformation and malinformation, spread with or without any intention to inflict harm on another entity."
estimates.page_loc: Table 4, 'Socio-demographic profiles of the respondents (N = 869)', row 'Action taken on suspicious news', Section 4.1, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure respondent self-report with no external verification of anything shared. The study's fake-news definition was printed at the head of Section B of the questionnaire before respondents answered; the 'suspicious news' item is nonetheless the respondent's own judgement of suspiciousness, not a verified falsity coding.
estimates.moderator_quote: Section B: The fake news definition (Section 2.1) begins Section B, followed by an instruction to answer the questions based on the respondents' personal experiences since January 2020 (i.e., coincides with the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic). // Forty-two undergraduate students assisted with the data collection by disseminating the Google Form link through social media platforms including Facebook and WhatsApp.
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE, flagged for adjudication. (1) The numerator is 'suspicious news', i.e. content the respondent themselves finds dubious, not content verified false - it is a proxy for misinformation sharing, not a direct measure. (2) It is a single-choice item, so it counts only those whose FIRST response is to forward; someone who verifies and then shares false content is not counted, which biases the figure downward. (3) The paper's actual fake-news-sharing measure (five 4-point Likert items including 'I have shared/spread fake news before knowingly' and '... unknowingly') is never reported as a share of respondents - only Cronbach's alpha 0.823, factor loadings and SEM paths - so no row can be built from it (scale means/loadings only, no share; see the instructions' exclusion of scale-mean-only reporting). (4) Convenience sample recruited by 42 undergraduates through their own Facebook/WhatsApp networks: 80.6% students, mean age 22.7, rural and offline Malaysians excluded by the authors' own admission; population_scope coded general_public because eligibility was any Malaysian aged 18+, but the realised sample is a young student convenience sample. (5) topic coded general_news: the pandemic supplies the time frame ('since January 2020'), not a content restriction; an adjudicator could defensibly code covid19 given the paper's framing. (6) Fieldwork dates are never stated; year 2020 is inferred from the recall window opening in January 2020 and the 28 Feb 2021 submission date. QUOTE NOTE: the text rendering interleaves the two printed columns, so the longest contiguous verbatim span carrying the value is the table cell itself, 'Share/Forward 19 2.2'. The full printed table row reads: Action taken on suspicious news - Ignore 283 (32.6), Share/Forward immediately 19 (2.2), Fact checking website 245 (28.2), Google verification 209 (24.1), Family/friends verification 112 (12.9); the five options sum to 100.0%.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately NOT extracted: (a) 'Frequency of sharing news (real/fake)': Never 101 (11.6%), Seldom 482 (55.5%), Occasionally 206 (23.7%), Frequently 80 (9.2%), summarised in the text as 'Most of the respondents in our sample actively shared news (88.4 %) compared to those who never do so (11.6 %)'. The 88.4% is the share who share NEWS OF ANY KIND, explicitly 'regardless of its veracity' - it is not a misinformation share and would be a serious over-count if treated as one. (b) 'Can identify fake news while reading?' Yes 38.8% / No 11.7% / Unsure 49.5%, and 'Aware of fact checking website in Malaysia?' Yes 41.9% - self-efficacy and awareness, not exposure or sharing. (c) 'Definition of fake news?' Yes 88.8% - knowledge item. (d) The intro cites external figures ('almost half (46 %) of the United Kingdom population were found to be exposed to COVID-19 related fake news [5]'; 'more than 25 % of the most watched YouTube videos on COVID-19 contained false or misleading information, reaching over 62 million views [6]'; '270 fake news related investigations since January 2020'): these are figures the paper cites from elsewhere and are barred by R8. (e) The SEM output (R2 = 49.2%, betas for Altruism 0.333, Ignorance 0.165, Entertainment 0.139) is association, not prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online self-administered questionnaire in English, piloted on 42 students, then distributed as a Google Form by 42 undergraduates through their own social media (Facebook, WhatsApp) over a ten-day window as a graded course exercise. 869 valid responses; eligibility Malaysians aged 18+; no sampling frame, no response rate, and no fieldwork dates reported - a self-selected convenience/snowball sample skewed to students (80.6%), female (59.7%) and young (mean 22.7, SD 6.13). Rural and offline Malaysians excluded (acknowledged limitation). Measures: four-point forced-choice Likert (no midpoint); fake-news-sharing scale alpha = 0.823; motive scales alpha 0.863-0.935; AVE and Fornell-Larcker discriminant validity established; Harman single-factor 28.7% and VIF 1.10-3.86 for common-method bias; PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. No behavioural or verified data of any kind; every measure is self-report. The one extracted prevalence figure comes from a descriptive sample-profile table, not from the study's own validated scale.
rob.item6_quote: The present study redefines fake news as "misleading or incorrect information in any forms, disseminated intentionally or unintentionally". In other words, fake news is deemed to encompass misinformation, disinformation and malinformation, spread with or without any intention to inflict harm on another entity.
